# Frameworks: Walter Murch

Built from the extract notes of 79 sources (59 of them carry his own words: interviews, masterclasses, Q&As, his essays and his books as quoted in them), dated 1998 to 2026. 24 frameworks, ordered by how many sources use each. "Sources" counts distinct sources where the idea appears (ids listed). Names are his where he named them; otherwise a short name marked *(unnamed)*. The How-to-score lines are scoring guidance for the council built from his own thresholds, not quotes. For any single-cut question, start with the Rule of Six (15): it is his best-known tool and the seat's core question, even though it is less often discussed than his working methods.

---

## 1. Cost threshold and tool adoption *(unnamed; "a threshold was passed" (S074) is his phrase)*
- **What it is:** Judge a new post-production tool by what its price does to the way you work, not by the time it promises to save. When media and stations become nearly free, you stop rationing: more stations, assistants get to cut, experiments cost nothing. But the work expands, so post does not get cheaper or shorter.
- **Parts:** (1) Price the change: with Avid he rationed two to four systems; with Final Cut he simply added a Mac, four stations for the price of one Avid (S072, S074). (2) Expect no net time saving: "saving time is fine in theory, but in practice it usually doesn't work that way." (S079) (3) Expect more footage: digital is easier for the director and harder for the editor (S018, S024). (4) Adopt by diving in for a couple of days to look for hidden problems, reading up, then asking editors who already cut on it (S023). (5) Keep the method, change the chisel: "I would make those same decisions today; I would just achieve them through different technologies." (S033) (6) Watch vendor lock-in: Apple dropped Final Cut under him in 2011 (S055); he values alternative systems (S073).
- **When to use:** Choosing an editing system, in-house versus post house, how many edit stations and assistants, how to budget post on a cheaper toolset.
- **How to score:** High if the lower cost per seat is spent on more people and more experiments, and working users of the tool were asked first. Low if the case rests on "it will save time" or bets the show on one closed vendor. (guidance, inferred from S053, S074, S079)
- **View over time:** In 1968 he saw a computer editing system and expected electronic editing everywhere within five years; it took about 20 (S023, 2015; S059, 2026). Newer (2025): post-production is not cheaper today, he says, because "work expands to fill the area available" (S053).
- **Quote:** "compared to working with film, the experience of working digitally is that it's free" (S074)
- **Sources:** 14 (S017, S018, S020, S023, S024, S033, S051, S053, S055, S059, S072, S073, S074, S079)

## 2. The dailies memory system *(unnamed)*
- **What it is:** The editor's defense against forgetting. Everything is seen once, in the dark, with fresh eyes; each reaction is written down with the reason; one frame per setup goes on the wall. Nothing sinks, and shots that a search tool would never pair can collide by chance.
- **Parts:** Watch all dailies and free-associate timecoded notes, often in two passes (S016, S029). Never write only good or no good: write why, and tag takes so you can find them months later (S017, S053). Mark the one frame per setup that answers why they shot it (S020, S057). Print stills on boards, about 25 a page, and keep them on the walls (S016, S035, S055). Highlight keepers and avoid-list in different colors and build the first assembly from the keepers (S016, S053). Keep a continuous roll of everything shot for a scene (S016, S053). For multi-camera or improvised coverage, grid every line against every camera and grade the cells (S018, S051). Detailed notes let assistants cut scenes with his eyes (S073). Boards and notes create the random collisions that random-access systems do not (S024).
- **When to use:** Every shooting day, and above all when volume is high: multi-camera series, documentary, digital takes with many resets.
- **How to score:** 5 if someone on the post team saw every take once and the notes say why; 3 if notes exist but only say good or bad; 1 if footage goes straight to the timeline unseen. He says skipping dailies only works when "the film is short enough and simple enough" (S053).
- **Quote:** "You’re only going to see this material for the first time once" (S016)
- **Sources:** 13 (S016, S017, S018, S019, S020, S024, S029, S035, S051, S053, S055, S057, S073)

## 3. Metaphoric sound (reassociation) *(his term)*
- **What it is:** Sound that does not literally match the picture opens a gap the audience fills with its own meaning. The further the sound sits from the image, the more dimension the scene gains, until the thread snaps.
- **Steps:** Strip the literal sounds. Choose the sound for what the character feels, not for what the object is (the Godfather door had to close with finality, S004, S058). Place a detached sound against the picture, like the elevated train before the Solozzo killing (S018, S057): "the sound that Michael Corleone's neurons are making" (S055). Keep sound and picture at right angles, not playing the same note (S049, S056). Push hard, and back off only if the film pushes back (S077).
- **When to use:** A scene's inner state is not reading; a picture problem will not yield; the picture budget is gone. Sound is "much less expensive than image" (S020).
- **How to score:** 5 if the sound adds what the picture cannot show and the audience can still connect it; 3 if literal and clean; 1 if it duplicates the picture (on the nose) or is so far off the image that the connection breaks. (guidance, inferred from S004, S077)
- **Quote:** "Once you stray into metaphoric sound, which is simply sound that does not match what you’re looking at, the human mind will look for deeper and deeper patterns." (S002)
- **Sources:** 12 (S001, S002, S004, S018, S020, S049, S055, S056, S057, S058, S077, S079)

## 4. Peaks and valleys *(unnamed; his image)*
- **What it is:** Impact comes from contrast. Big sound lands only after small sound, and silence is the strongest and most dangerous tool, used a few times a film with a controlled slope.
- **Parts:** Plan two or three near-silent valleys per film (S079), or three or four unexpected silences (S081). Know the kind of silence: locational, psychological, or impossible (S002). Control the slope into it, because too fast feels like a broken theater and too slow loses the tension (S002, S081). Put the tiniest sounds inside a silence to make it sharper (S011). Pulse the format: long stretches of mono, opening to full surround only at the big moments, then back (S052, S059). Remove the expected sound at the peak (the silent scream in Godfather III, S004; the lake in Godfather II, S078).
- **When to use:** Shaping the sound of a film or an episode, deciding where the mix money goes, any scene that feels loud but not strong.
- **How to score:** High if valleys are planned before the peaks; low if density and loudness stay constant: "A monotonously dense soundtrack is just as wearing as a monotonously loud film." (S001)
- **Quote:** "If there are no valleys, then it doesn't matter how high the mountains actually are; they won't seem high." (S079)
- **Sources:** 11 (S001, S002, S004, S011, S026, S052, S059, S078, S079, S080, S081)

## 5. Point of view: single, divergent, convergent *(his terms)*
- **What it is:** Every story with several characters is told from a single point of view, diverges from one group, or converges from separate strands. Name which one you have, then cut to its rules.
- **Parts:** Single: every shot is the lead or what he sees, which makes an unappealing lead work because the audience has no escape (S018, S026, S056, S058, S079). Divergent: introduce everyone together, then scatter them (S050). Convergent: intercut two stories that later meet (S050). A passive lead needs a witness or narrator so the audience has access, and if you take care of that lens character you take care of the audience (S006, S052, S058). In a contested true story, ask who is telling it and whether the audience cares about that person (S013, S019).
- **When to use:** Script notes before shooting, pilot structure, a documentary on disputed history, any film with an unlikable lead.
- **How to score:** High if the point-of-view type is clear and the cut obeys it; low if it drifts, or an unsympathetic lead is given escape valves that release the audience. (guidance, inferred from S018, S050)
- **Quote:** "you can look at every screenplay every story and say with multiple characters is this story convergent divergent or single point of view" (S050)
- **Sources:** 10 (S006, S013, S018, S019, S026, S050, S052, S056, S058, S079)

## 6. Music channels emotion, it does not create it *(unnamed; "musical steroids" is his image, S055)*
- **What it is:** Drama builds an emotional charge; well-placed music grounds it and tells the audience what to do with it. Music used to manufacture emotion is a steroid.
- **Parts:** (1) Make the scene work on drama first (S002, S055). (2) Keep the freedom to use music or not at any moment; heavy early music makes the film dependent (S002). (3) Keep music sideways to the picture; mirroring it is on the nose, which is why an all-Doors score failed on Apocalypse Now (S052). (4) For tension, leave music out (S055, S032). (5) Temp music mixes its DNA with the film; best is none, and if used, expect a painful swap (S019, S050, S055). (6) Bring the composer on early, ideally during the shoot; music is "like another actor in the scene" (S050). (7) Separate source music in the scene from underscoring (S080). (8) Music asks less of an audience than abstract sound (S057); it can work as an emotional cutaway (S017).
- **When to use:** Spotting sessions, temp-track decisions, when to hire the composer, music budget.
- **How to score:** High if the scene plays without music and music only modulates it; low if music has to supply the emotion or comments directly on the image. (guidance, inferred from S002, S052)
- **Quote:** "if you use music to create the emotion, rather than to modulate or channel emotion already created by the drama itself, you are using music the way athletes use steroids" (S002)
- **Sources:** 9 (S002, S017, S019, S032, S050, S052, S055, S057, S080)

## 7. Abundance of events, paucity of coverage (documentary) *(his phrase)*
- **What it is:** Fiction has fixed events and too many interpretations: six setups and seven takes give 42 readings of every line (S057). Documentary is the reverse: many events, thin coverage. So in documentary the editor chooses which notes get played at all and is, in effect, a writer.
- **Steps:** Know which abundance you have (S018, S020, S057). Build one chronological timeline per strand, weave them into one long timeline, then cut it down (Coup 53: four timelines, an 8.5-hour weave, S019). Agitate the material until scenes clump (S051). Pick who tells the story; there is no God's-eye view (S013, S019). Back every claim with several sources and a visual, and fill gaps with animation rather than fake recreation (S013). Bend reality only a little, to show the essence (S033, S034). The documentary editor helps write the film and should get a writing credit (S016, S019).
- **When to use:** Any unscripted, archive or reality project, a making-of, or a scripted show built from heavy improvisation.
- **How to score:** 5 if there is a clear teller, sourced claims, and the editor has writing authority; 1 if hundreds of hours are being cut with no point of view, or facts are invented to fill holes. (guidance, inferred from S013, S019, S034)
- **Quote:** "Whereas on a documentary, you are deciding what notes are going to get played in the first place." (S019)
- **Sources:** 9 (S013, S016, S018, S019, S020, S033, S034, S051, S057)

## 8. The scene-card wall *(unnamed)*
- **What it is:** One card per scene on the wall. Color is the scene's emotional tone, size is its weight, thin cards are connective tissue, a card turned into a diamond is a pivot. You read the shape of the whole film at a glance.
- **Parts:** Five or six words per card at most (S017). Choose the color fast and do not reconsider it (S019). Scan for runs of one color and break them up, as with "too much blue" in The English Patient (S019). Expect six or seven diamonds in a film (S019, S067). Group scenes into sequences, roughly 36 to 50 in a feature (S009). Add a purple "grace" card where the audience needs to breathe (S018). Put a red tag on each card once it is assembled; the job is to tag them all (S057). He used colored cards for the 532 hours of Coup 53 (S013) and still maps films with stills and notes on walls (S035).
- **When to use:** Tracking the assembly, restructuring, deciding which scenes can go, showing a director or producer the shape of the film or season.
- **How to score:** High if the wall shows clear pivots and a varied emotional color; low if there are long single-color runs or no pivot you can point to. (guidance, inferred from S017, S019)
- **Quote:** "In any film, there are probably six or seven of those diamond-scenes." (S019)
- **Sources:** 8 (S009, S013, S017, S018, S019, S035, S057, S067)

## 9. Build first, then the plateau test *(unnamed)*
- **What it is:** Montage means to build. Get to a whole assembly fast, with "eyes half-closed" (S017), without trying to fix the film yet. Then make pass after pass until the edits seem to trigger themselves. That plateau is when a scene is done for now.
- **Steps:** Just begin; the first step shrinks the mountain (S019, S067). Move from good piece to good piece (S053). Do not fix the film in the first assembly (S017). Build it before cutting it down (S056). Aim for speed to a full assembly (S057). Then list changes, redo, and repeat; by the third or fourth pass the cuts feel inevitable (S059). A scene cut before its neighbors exist is "shadow boxing"; stop at the plateau and wait (S059). Inspiration follows work, not waiting (S020).
- **When to use:** Scheduling the assembly, deciding when a scene, episode or cut is done, judging whether an editor is polishing too early.
- **How to score:** Done when edits feel self-triggered after three or four passes; not done while each pass still yields structural notes; over-worked if a scene is fine-cut before the scenes around it exist. (guidance, inferred from S017, S059)
- **Quote:** "I will reach a point where I kind of forget that I made those edits." (S059)
- **Sources:** 8 (S017, S019, S020, S053, S056, S057, S059, S067)

## 10. Another rule of three (disagreeing with the director) *(his phrase)*
- **What it is:** The editor is paid for ideas and should challenge the director. Pitch a real idea once; if it is refused, drop it; raise it again at another moment; a third time if it truly matters; then stop and serve the director's version.
- **Steps:** Contribute ideas, do not wait for orders (S018, S035). Make suggestions at the right moments, not constantly (S055). After three refusals, let go; the final call is the director's prerogative (S018, S053, S079). Adapt to the director's working style: Coppola left him alone, Bigelow sat in the room daily (S022). The exception is a crisis: when Coppola proposed shelving The Conversation, Murch asked to try his ideas first, and they saved it (S049).
- **When to use:** Any creative disagreement in post, including with a showrunner, producer or platform executive.
- **How to score:** Healthy if ideas are voiced and dropped after three tries; unhealthy if the editor is silent or a pest. (guidance, inferred from S018, S053)
- **Quote:** "My rule of thumb for places where there's a disagreement between you, the editor, and the director is another rule of three." (S053)
- **Sources:** 7 (S018, S022, S035, S049, S053, S055, S079)

## 11. Nodal editing: where and on what frame to cut *(his term)*
- **What it is:** A shot has a grain like wood; you can only cut at a node, where the action has become inevitable but is not yet complete. The last frame of the outgoing shot should be iconic, because each cut works like a flashbulb that burns that frame into memory.
- **Parts:** Cut when the action is inevitable: wheels up, door about to close (S018, S020). Do not let a character finish an action and then cut, unless the action is the point (S018). Cut just before a shot overstays, or just before attention flags (S018, S049). For a walk: two steps, cut on the uplift of the third (S012). Choose the last frame for what it reveals; he calls it the most important part of the editor's performance (S017, S020, S051). Do not cut on matching action by reflex; it creates a stutter and fights the flashbulb (S016, S020, S049).
- **When to use:** Fine-cutting, and diagnosing why a scene feels sluggish or stuttery.
- **How to score:** High if cuts land on rising potential with revealing out-frames; low if actions are completed in both shots or shots outstay their interest. (guidance, inferred from S018, S020)
- **Quote:** "And that moment of inevitability is the moment of the cut." (S020)
- **Sources:** 7 (S012, S016, S017, S018, S020, S049, S051)

## 12. Assemble with the sound off *(unnamed)*
- **What it is:** Cut the first assembly as a silent film, lip-reading and imagining the sound, so the recorded dialogue does not imprison the imagination. Then turn the sound on: most of it fits, some is broken, and a share is a lucky accident worth keeping.
- **Steps:** Notes, then a silent cut, refined more than once (S012). Turn the sound on; fix what is broken, such as words cut mid-syllable, and keep the accidents (S012, S017). Then add dialogue, key effects, temp music and rough final music in that order (S079).
- **When to use:** First assembly of each scene. He says it is his habit, borrowed from David Lean, and Dede Allen did the opposite (S017, S057).
- **How to score:** A scene that reads from faces and bodies with the sound off will hold; one that needs the words to make sense has a weak picture cut. (guidance, inferred from S017, S067)
- **View over time:** His split when the sound comes on: 70 percent fine, 10 wrong, 15 interesting (S012, 2016); about 75 percent right (S055, 2018); newer, 70 right, 15 wrong, 15 fortuitous (S057, 2026). The method stayed the same.
- **Quote:** "If I had the sound up, that would be the sound and it would crowd out the possibility for other sounds." (S011)
- **Sources:** 7 (S011, S012, S017, S055, S057, S067, S079)

## 13. Dense Clarity, Clear Density (the Law of Two-and-a-Half) *(his names)*
- **What it is:** Three of anything of one sound "color" merge into a group. In any five-second moment an audience follows about two and a half layers of one color, or up to five spread across the spectrum from speech to music. Beyond that you get density without clarity.
- **Steps:** Place each track on the spectrum from encoded (speech) to embodied (music), with effects between (S001, S002). Spread layers across the spectrum instead of stacking one color (S001). Mix the dialogue first, alone, then add the next most dominant layer while listening to what is there (S001, S002). To add a layer, take one away (S001, S002). Past three units of one kind, stop syncing each one and get the group right (S001, S002). Vary density with the story (S001). The same limit applies to ideas: an audience processes about two and a half thematic elements at once (S071, S079).
- **When to use:** Any mix, especially action and crowd scenes; also any scene or episode trying to carry too many threads at once.
- **How to score:** Count layers per five seconds: five or fewer across colors, two and a half or fewer in one color, reads clear; above that, noise. His thresholds, not laws: "five layers is a threshold which should not be surpassed thoughtlessly" (S001).
- **Quote:** "five layers is the maximum that can be tolerated by an audience if you also want them to maintain a clear sense of the individual elements that are contributing to the mix" (S002)
- **Sources:** 7 (S001, S002, S003, S006, S067, S071, S079)

## 14. Digestion and transitions *(unnamed; the five levels of transition are his)*
- **What it is:** An audience is force-fed and needs moments to digest; logic and emotion digest on separate tracks. The bigger the transition, the more aware the audience is of it, so build up to it and give time to absorb it.
- **Parts:** Five levels of transition: frame, cut, scene, act, and the film's beginning and end (S081). At a scene transition, hold the last outgoing shot about 30 percent longer than an internal cut (S081). After a shock, give the audience time before the next scene (S081). Build grace notes: humor, a silent face, a breathing scene (S018). Bleed scenes with pre-laps and post-laps (S018, S081). Change sound texture at the scene cut, where audiences notice it (S053); let sound carry jumps in time and place (S066). Never dissolve to mark time or escape an awkward cut (S081). Think of the emotional curve of the whole film, not the jugular every time (S049). Fast cutting as a general style costs comprehension (S025). Moving one transition has consequences down the line (S067).
- **When to use:** Pacing notes, act breaks and episode endings, any preview that reports confusion or exhaustion.
- **How to score:** High if each big turn has a build-up, a held beat and a breath after; low if the cut is relentless or dissolves are used as patches. (guidance, inferred from S018, S081)
- **Quote:** "if you feed people too fast, they feel like the stuff is being rammed down their throat and they’re going to choke." (S018)
- **Sources:** 7 (S018, S025, S049, S053, S066, S067, S081)

## 15. The Rule of Six *(his name)*
- **What it is:** Six things a cut should do, ranked: emotion, story, rhythm, eye-trace, the two-dimensional plane of the screen, and three-dimensional space. In the book he weights them 51, 23, 10, 7, 5 and 4 percent, so emotion outweighs the other five together (S067). When one cut cannot do all six, let go from the bottom.
- **Steps:** Ask what emotion this cut should carry, whether it is the correct one, and how it relates to the scenes before and after (S025). Check the story still reads. Check rhythm. Check eye-trace, where about 90 percent of the audience is looking (S049). Continuity of screen direction and space comes last (S017, S049). Drop items from the bottom up; if one of the top three must go, rhythm goes first (S017). You may drop story for pure emotion briefly, like astronauts weightless for 45 seconds, then land back on story (S017). You may confuse the audience slightly, but not for long (S049).
- **When to use:** Every cut decision, and every argument about a mistake where a continuity error buys emotional truth.
- **How to score:** Score a cut by the highest item it serves and the highest it breaks. Breaking only spatial continuity to keep emotion is a good trade; breaking emotion to keep continuity is a bad one. (guidance, inferred from S017, S067)
- **View over time:** He calls the weights "slightly tongue-in-cheek" (S067) and says he "had to make the numbers jump around" (S017, 2020). Newer (2026): the list is a self-correction for an analytical editor like him; a purely emotional editor would need to be reminded that technique matters (S059). That matches the book's introduction, which frames its advice as warnings to himself (S002).
- **Quote:** "my recommendation is to let go from the bottom of the list up." (S017)
- **Sources:** 6 (S017, S025, S029, S049, S059, S067)

## 16. Hit the same frame twice *(unnamed)*
- **What it is:** Choose the cut point by feel at running speed, never by scrubbing. Run the shot, stop at the moment the cut feels right, note the frame, repeat. The same frame twice means the cut is right; the spread of misses teaches the film's rhythmic signature.
- **Steps:** Play at 24 frames a second with a hand on the key, thinking the audience's thoughts; stop; read the timecode; rewind and repeat (S011, S017, S020). Never scrub to find the out-frame (S017, S020). He pushed Adobe to add real-time trimming to Premiere (S008, S012). He uses the blink version of this test on himself and says he will retire when he can no longer pass it (S036). He stands to edit to feel the rhythm (S011, S012).
- **When to use:** Fine cut, a disputed cut point in review, training a junior editor.
- **How to score:** Two hits on the same frame: keep. Misses spread across several frames: the cut is uncertain; look again. (guidance from his own test, S017)
- **Quote:** "If I hit the same frame twice in a row, that tells me that’s probably a good cut point, because it’s impossible to do that, to hit that same frame, in any other way than musically." (S017)
- **Sources:** 6 (S008, S011, S012, S017, S020, S036)

## 17. Cut on the blink *(from In the Blink of an Eye)*
- **What it is:** A blink marks the moment a thought is complete. An actor fully in character blinks where the thought ends, so that is where the cut belongs.
- **Rules:** Cut a frame or two before the blink, and only if the actor is in character; cut just after for a double-take stutter; never cut during it; override it when your own rhythm says so (S016). It fits quiet dialogue, not action (S058). Blinks reveal thought: he counts politicians' blink rates as a hobby (S036). Whether the blink causes the break in thought or follows it is, by his account, a hunch (S016).
- **When to use:** Dialogue close-ups and judging a performance in dailies.
- **How to score:** In quiet dialogue, cuts on thought-ends read invisible; cuts mid-thought feel awkward, since "If the audience is not ready, the cut will feel awkward." (S081)
- **Quote:** "When we get an idea, we tend to blink" (S029)
- **Sources:** 6 (S016, S029, S036, S058, S067, S071)

## 18. A director of photography for sound *(his phrase)*
- **What it is:** The director needs one person to talk to about the whole sound, as they talk to the DP about the image. That person designs and mixes, and runs a three-legged race with the picture editor from the assembly on.
- **Parts:** One sound lead who can both design and mix (S004, S079). Avoid the old Hollywood split between sound editing and re-recording, which he compares to separating the lighting director from the camera operator (S077). Sketch key sound moments during the assembly, skip Foley detail, hand off early (S053). Keep picture and sound feeding each other; ideally the composer is on during the shoot (S050). He does not like locking picture and handing it over (S050). On one person doing both picture and sound: "I think it’s not something that will become the norm, simply because you have to have interests in both areas." (S024) Power on a film goes to whoever controls a bottleneck (S004).
- **When to use:** Hiring post staff, deciding whether the editor also handles sound, setting when sound work starts.
- **How to score:** High if the sound lead starts before picture lock and sound is sketched in the assembly; low if locked picture is thrown over the wall to a separate department. (guidance, inferred from S050, S053)
- **Quote:** "it's a three-legged race between you, the editor, picture editor, and the sound designer" (S053)
- **Sources:** 6 (S004, S024, S050, S053, S077, S079)

## 19. The length budget: time the script, then the thirty percent rule *(the thirty percent rule is his rule of thumb)*
- **What it is:** Predict running time before cutting, and read an assembly's length as a diagnosis. Up to 30 percent over the release length comes down with trims; more than that needs structural surgery.
- **Steps:** Read the script at speed, tick what is good or bad, then write notes that might save time or money (S050). Time every scene with a stopwatch, speaking the lines and pacing the moves, twice; about two days a script (S017, S050). Compare with the script supervisor's timings; the five or six scenes that differ most are the questions for the director (S017, S050). Feed edited scene lengths into a running database; within about ten days of shooting he knows how long the assembly will be (S050). Judge the material's "water content": dense footage is harder to reduce than redundant coverage (S040). Mind the ceiling: past about two hours a film "begins to turn into something else" (S017); one writer reports his drop-dead length as about 145 minutes (S006, paraphrase).
- **When to use:** Before greenlight, when setting the shoot and post schedule, at every assembly review; for series, against the episode slot.
- **How to score:** 30 percent or less over: trim scenes. More than 30 percent: lose scenes or storylines. Even when every scene is good, cut for fatigue (S040). (thresholds his, S050, S071)
- **Quote:** "if it's more than 30% you have to do surgery" (S050)
- **Sources:** 5 (S006, S017, S040, S050, S071)

## 20. Heart scenes and umbilical cords *(his image)*
- **What it is:** Some scenes are the heart of the film. Others are umbilical cords: they fed the project, often they were the director's way in, and once the film is born they can be cut. To find them, cut the scene that seems most essential and see what the others carry, like a DP switching off the key light.
- **Steps:** Ask of each threatened scene: heart or umbilical cord (S017, S050). Run the key-light test: remove the scene that seems most important and watch (S017). Be suspicious of scenes that state their message too directly (S025). Check payoffs far away: a removed scene may hold up the ending, as in Ghost (S017). If a pivot scene goes, build a new pivot (S017). The test case is Julia: the director's favorite scene went after previews, and the audience found its footing sooner (S025, S050, S058).
- **When to use:** Over length, previews show no traction at the start, a director or writer defends a favorite scene.
- **How to score:** Cut if the film closes over the gap and nothing later depends on it; keep if a payoff or pivot downstream needs it. (guidance, inferred from S017, S050)
- **Quote:** "certain scenes are heart scenes and other scenes are like umbilical cords." (S017)
- **Sources:** 4 (S017, S025, S050, S058)

## 21. Referred pain (reading previews) *(his term, borrowed from medicine)*
- **What it is:** A preview moves you "90 degrees off-center" (S017) and shows your blind spots. But the audience names a symptom; the cause usually sits somewhere else in the film.
- **Steps:** Watch with a full room; the main thing a theater gives is other people watching (S059). Note where the audience loses traction (S058). Trace the complaint upstream, from elbow to shoulder (S017). Where they are emotionally confused, give them time, as with the snow shots added to Cold Mountain (S081). Expect a very good preview to scare a studio, because it loses control of the film (S059).
- **When to use:** Test screenings, platform or broadcaster notes, festival or buyer feedback.
- **How to score:** A fix is right when it addresses the upstream cause and the next screening gets traction sooner. (guidance, inferred from S017, S058)
- **Quote:** "the problem is not in the elbow. It’s somewhere else." (S017)
- **Sources:** 4 (S017, S058, S059, S081)

## 22. Assemble it yourself, then let the machine vary it (AI) *(unnamed)*
- **What it is:** The editor learns the film by assembling it. If AI is used, it comes after: the human assembles, then asks the machine to try it another way and keeps what is good.
- **Steps:** Assemble by hand, because "when you assemble a film yourself you learn the film." (S058) Then use the machine for variations. Watch for its fingerprints, a smell "that is not your smell" (S058). Expect to reinvent the method for every film (S058).
- **When to use:** Deciding whether to use AI assembly, how to staff assistants, how to budget post with AI tools.
- **How to score:** High if a person made the first assembly and AI explores options; low if AI replaces the first viewing. (guidance, inferred from S053, S058)
- **View over time:** 2020: "yeah it's already happening" (S050). March 2025: too early to tell, but as big as the coming of sound, and he had used AI only for text (S053). May 2025: the assemble-then-vary sweet spot, offered as "early early days" (S058). Newest, October 2026: "We just don't know." (S057), and he calls AI "television cubed" (S057).
- **Quote:** "It may be that you do the assembly and then you put it in and you say do this a different way." (S058)
- **Sources:** 4 (S050, S053, S057, S058)

## 23. ADR that sounds like production *(unnamed)*
- **What it is:** When set sound is unusable, replace it, but make clean studio dialogue sound like it was recorded on location, and schedule it by arithmetic.
- **Parts:** Schedule about eight lines per hour: lines per actor times actors, divided by eight (S050). Use the same type of microphone as the set, hide it so the actor is "naked with the image", baffle the room (S050, S052). Roll off the low end and damage it slightly (S052, S055). Make actors truly shout when the scene shouts (S050). On Apocalypse Now nearly all dialogue was ADR: 92 percent in one telling (S052), 98 in another (S006).
- **When to use:** Budgeting and scheduling ADR, deciding between ADR and fixing production sound.
- **How to score:** ADR that sounds too clean fails; flag any line that sounds like a studio. (guidance, inferred from S052, S055)
- **Quote:** "in general I schedule about eight lines of ADR per hour of recording time" (S050)
- **Sources:** 4 (S006, S050, S052, S055)

## 24. Three legs of the stool (choosing a project) *(his image)*
- **What it is:** Take a project when three things hold: the material resonates and pushes you past your comfort zone, the director and team are right, and there is enough time and money. Any two are almost enough; a missing leg is a warning.
- **Steps:** Read the screenplay at speed and write notes (S050). Meet the director and trade ideas over lunch (S075). If they cannot give you the script, assume there are problems with it (S050). His counter-example is Tomorrowland: he started without a finished script, worked 15 months, was let go, and says the judgement was wrong (S016, S050, S067).
- **When to use:** Taking on a project, hiring a key post person, entering a co-production.
- **How to score:** Three legs: go. Two: go with the risk named. One: decline. (thresholds his, S050)
- **Quote:** "those three things are important any two of those are almost enough" (S050)
- **Sources:** 1 states it (S050); 3 more apply it (S016, S067, S075)

# Positions: Walter Murch

Built from the five batch notes on 79 sources (interviews, masterclasses, articles and his own essays, 1996 to 2026). 39 topics, ordered by how many sources support them, with business decisions in editing and post-production weighted first among equals. Each stance has a verbatim quote, source id and date (YouTube upload date for videos; "c." marks a year taken from the text when `sources.md` lists the source as undated). Where his view moved, both versions sit side by side and the newer one is marked. Topics with no evidence say so.

## Restoring, recutting and the director's written intent (10 sources)
- **Stance:** When you reopen a finished film, follow the author's documented intent and interpret only the gaps; new material must rebalance the structure, not just add. Leave your own finished work alone.
- **Evidence:**
  - Touch of Evil (1998): "we held ourselves strictly to what was in the memos" (S078, c.1998) "At that point I had to interpret what Welles might have wanted." (S080, c.1999)
  - "Every film should have a document like this as a kind of touchstone" (S078, c.1998)
  - Apocalypse Now Redux: "The new scenes balance things in a structural sense." (S066, 2012-08) but "Kilgore tipped the balance of the film toward him, away from Kurtz" (S066, 2012-08)
  - Scope creep: "it evolved from a very small seed a DVD extra for France only into Apocalypse Now redux" (S050, 2020-03)
  - Restoring a cut moment for Apocalypse Now Final Cut: "and so you've removed the very thing that was predicted at the beginning of the film" (S050, 2020-03)
  - His own work: "I keep myself from saying those things or thinking those things." (S056, 2022-02) After remastering The Conversation: "I don’t think my approach has fundamentally changed." (S016, 2020-04)
- **Read:** a written brief outlives its author and settles arguments later; a recut is a structural decision with losses as well as gains. Inferred from S002, S017, S033, S050, S052, S066, S078, S080.

## Running time, assembly length and cutting down (9 sources)
- **Stance:** Expect the first assembly to run long. Up to 30% over the target trims by diet and exercise; beyond that the film needs surgery. Past about two hours a film turns into something else. Cut even excellent material when length starts to tire the audience.
- **Evidence:**
  - "an assembly should be no more than thirty percent over the ideal running length of the film" (S071, 2005-11)
  - "my rule of thumb is that if my first assembly is thirty percent longer than the release of the film then it's easy to get to that time" (S050, 2020-03) "if it's more than 30% you have to do surgery" (S050, 2020-03)
  - "When a film gets over two hours, it begins to turn into something else." (S017, 2020-02)
  - "It's like, you know, a 12-course meal, each course is delicious, but by the eighth course, oh, another delicious meal, you know?" (S040, c.2016)
  - "it was clear that you couldn't release a four and a half hour version of Ripley. It had to be cut down." (S040, c.2016)
- **Over time:** 2016-02, a writer reports his drop-dead length for most films as about 145 minutes (paraphrase, S006). 2020-02 (newer), the limit is two to two and a half hours because the audience's hypnosis has a physical limit (S017). Same view, stated more firmly.
- **Cases:** The Conversation's first assembly ran four and a half hours and came in under two (S053, S056); Cold Mountain went from five hours to 2:25 (reporter's account, S073); Ripley ran four and a half (S018).

## Studios, executives and who controls the cut (9 sources)
- **Stance:** Control sits with whoever holds a bottleneck. Show executives only finished-feeling work, expect them to resist new ideas, and offer help rather than defiance. Read executive anger as possible theater.
- **Evidence:**
  - "POWER on a film tends to gravitate toward those who control a bottleneck of some kind." (S004, undated)
  - "it was a rule of thumb throughout the industry never to let producers or studio executives hear the final mix unless it could be screened with an answer print." (S001, 2005-04)
  - "Naturally the studio, Universal again, was completely resistant to the idea." (S066, 2012-08)
  - "Welles was under no illusions as to who owned the film, but his approach was ‘I can help you make it better’." (S066, 2012-08)
  - "when a film really previews very well, the studio is sometimes frightened because it means they have no control over it anymore." (S059, 2026-05)
  - On a Paramount post chief yelling into a phone before hearing his request: "whatever I came in to ask for, I was going to now lower my ask because I didn't want that yelling at me." (S057, 2026-10)
  - Why Zoetrope left Los Angeles: "It was all done on a business level and we hated that." (S077, 2019-04)
- **Read:** he manages buyers by timing what they see, not by confrontation. Inferred from S001, S017 (Ghost dailies), S025 (Return to Oz left alone by Disney), S057, S059.

## Cost of tools and the economics of digital post (9 sources)
- **Stance:** The real change of digital was economic: media and machines became nearly free, so you stop rationing stations and let assistants practice. He has no nostalgia for what film cost.
- **Evidence:**
  - "compared to working with film, the experience of working digitally is that it's free" (S074, c.2016)
  - "The real advantage of something like Final Cut is that for the first time in the history of film, really, the cost of the media and the cost of the apparatus with which you manipulate the media are relevantly insignificant." (S024, 2006-06)
  - "It's good to have four burners on a stove when you're cooking dinner. You can put all of them to use" (S072, 2003)
  - "That Final Cut Pro was using off-the-shelf computers, it was not using any proprietary hardware" (S074, c.2016)
  - "Back in 1967, ten minutes of 35mm workprint cost $100." (S020, 2024-03) "a Moviola, that hunk of metal, was essential, but it was like buying a car." (S058, 2025-05)
  - "we're living in paradise, comparatively speaking, because of how those those costs have simply evaporated." (S053, 2025-03)
  - Particle Fever on film "would have had to have a a budget 10 times the size of the budget and an army of people in post-production." (S051, 2016-09)
- **Read:** cheaper per seat, not cheaper per film (see the next topics). Inferred from S053, S074, S079.

## Adopting new tools and timing the switch (8 sources)
- **Stance:** Early adopter, but tests for hidden problems and asks working editors before committing a feature. The goal outranks the tool. A vendor can drop you.
- **Evidence:**
  - "When anything new comes along, my nose immediately starts to twitch." (S059, 2026-05) "I will jump into these crocodile infested waters sooner than" (S055, 2018-06)
  - "I just dive into it. I do a couple of days exploring, just to make sure there aren’t any real hidden snakes in there." (S023, 2015-11) Before Premiere he asked Kirk Baxter, Angus Wall and the Coens (S023).
  - "It’s good that there are alternate systems out there, and I had my eye on Final Cut for a number of years." (S073, 2003-12)
  - "Apple pulled the rug out from under me in 2011" (S055, 2018-06)
  - "If you have something to say, you will find a method irrespective of the technology." (S079, c.1997)
  - "forces me to look at the way that I work and examine that; it also makes me look at the material in a slightly different way." (S073, 2003-12)
- **Over time:**
  - 1968: "I thought, this is great, electronic editing will be everywhere in five years." (S023, 2015-11)
  - 2015-11 (newer): "And in fact I was totally wrong, it wasn’t five years before we were editing like that, it was 20 years." (S023)
  - Film itself: "film will disappear. It’s not going to be with us for very much longer." (S016, 2020-04) Yet analog accidents produced cuts digital would have hidden, such as the Lawrence of Arabia match-to-sunrise (paraphrase, S020, 2024-03).
- **Read:** right about direction, wrong about timing by decades; he now pairs enthusiasm with a few days of risk checks. Inferred from S023, S059.

## Hiring, team size and assistants (8 sources)
- **Stance:** Hire for compatibility, rhythm and empathy. Size the team to the film and the editor's temperament. Let assistants cut scenes and listen to them.
- **Evidence:**
  - Asked what he values in colleagues: "Compatibility, but that covers a multitude of things." (S016, 2020-04)
  - "do you want to be a film editor do you have a sense of rhythm do you have a sense of how to tell a story and do you can you empathize with characters and with the audience" (S049, 2020-10)
  - "And so listen to your assistance because there's lots of good ideas circulating out there." (S053, 2025-03)
  - "it was very easy for me as an editor to allow my assistants to have practice editing." (S074, c.2016) Assistants cut from his notes so they "can look at it with my eyes and get a sense of what it is that I’m interested in." (S073, 2003-12)
  - Team size: "But even it's down to temperament." (S058, 2025-05) Apocalypse Now had about 45 people (S058); Particle Fever was "just me and the director in an editing room." (S051, 2016-09) "So I had to gear up my assistant chops to allow me to do the work that I need to do." (S034, undated)

## Working with directors: control, trust and many voices (8 sources)
- **Stance:** Adapt to each director's style. Trust given is repaid. He prefers directors who gather many points of view over a single uncompromised vision.
- **Evidence:**
  - "Kathryn Bigelow, on the other hand, was in the editing room every day from 9 to 5. And you just have to navigate those differences." (S022, 2025-04)
  - "Yes, a lot of trust, but the surprising thing about trust is, if you’re given all of this trust, you repay it" (S025, 2015-11)
  - "He gives heads of department, and the actors, a lot of rope. Paradoxically you then feel more beholden, given the trust he has extended to you." (S026, 2017-08) "He always gives us plenty of rope, sometimes enough to hang ourselves with." (S078, c.1998)
  - "The advantage of many points of view is that the work will be multifaceted, rather than monophonic" (S078, c.1998)
  - On a future where one person thinks a film into being, the tension is "total realisation of a private vision with no compromises" (S031, 2013-07); he doubts it would be good (article's paraphrase, S035).
  - "try to do all these things, but then surprise me, too." (S058, 2025-05)

## Shooting volume and more footage (7 sources)
- **Stance:** Digital makes shooting more cheap and easy, and moves the cost to the cutting room. More footage means removing good material.
- **Evidence:**
  - "It’s easier for the director, largely. And it’s somewhat easier for the script supervisor, but it’s harder for the editor." (S018, 2020-03)
  - Resets within one take: "I had a scene with 32 of those in a single take." (S022, 2025-04) "On Tomorrowland, the record was 35 resets within the same shot" (S020, 2024-03). The two counts differ.
  - "It complicates it !! But it can complicate it in a good way." (S020, 2024-03)
  - "You have to condense it, otherwise it's going to be too weak." (S040, c.2016)
  - Apocalypse Now: "they’d shot roughly a 100:1 ratio between film exposed to film used" (S066, 2012-08)
  - Resets hurt actors, like a trapeze act repeated without a break (paraphrase, S050, 2020-03); the trend is more hours of footage per editor (paraphrase, S024, 2006-06).

## Remote work and shared dailies (7 sources)
- **Stance:** He has cut a feature thousands of miles from its director and made it work. What he mourns is not the room but the communal screening of dailies, where a crew reads the film and each other.
- **Evidence:**
  - Cold Mountain, cut in Bucharest while Minghella shot in the Carpathians: "He’d look at them on his laptop and phone me up and talk about them." (S073, 2003-12) Dailies went out on DVD (S072, 2003).
  - "There was a communal part to the process that’s in danger of being completely lost." (S023, 2015-11)
  - "It’s a way of us all pickling ourselves in the juice of the film, and that’s gone now, with very few exception." (S016, 2020-04)
  - "you haven't really seen it and you haven't seen it in an environment where you can pick up subtle mood distinctions" (S050, 2020-03)
  - He wants dailies screenings back (paraphrase, S025, 2015-11).
- **Read:** remote is fine for cutting; it is costly for crew morale and shared judgment. Inferred from S016, S023, S050, S073.

## Picture and sound: one person or a handoff (7 sources)
- **Stance:** Picture and sound should feed each other until late. He dislikes locking picture and throwing it over the wall to sound, though he does not expect editor-sound designers to become the norm.
- **Evidence:**
  - "I absolutely don't like that system" (S050, 2020-03), on locked picture handed to sound with no way back.
  - "it's a three-legged race between you, the editor, picture editor, and the sound designer" (S053, 2025-03)
  - "it was a constant feedback from editing picture to editing sound" (S050, 2020-03)
  - "There was a specific problem in Hollywood sound in the very strict division between sound editing and sound re-recording" (S077, 2019-04)
  - The sound designer as "a director of photography for sound" (S079, c.1997)
  - "I think it’s not something that will become the norm, simply because you have to have interests in both areas." (S024, 2006-06)
  - On credits: "if anyone gets a credit of sound design on any of my films my credit becomes sound redesigner" (S052, 2016-03)

## Screens, formats and platforms (7 sources)
- **Stance:** Judge the work at the size the audience will see it, or imagine that size. Image quality matters only up to the point where emotion reads. Formats differ less creatively than vendors claim.
- **Evidence:**
  - "I had to find a way to imagine that screen to be 30 feet wide, rather than being five inches wide." (S024, 2006-06)
  - "the audience is not looking at the screen. They're looking into the screen." (S053, 2025-03)
  - "the amount of sonic density that could be tolerated and even enjoyed when the image was small, dim, fuzzy, and black and white was not the same when that image was big, bright, crisp, and in Technicolor" (S002, 2005)
  - "The quality of the image is almost irrelevant if it’s good enough for you to register the emotion on the actors’ faces." (S024, 2006-06)
  - "Creatively, the differences are minute, relatively speaking, between any of these systems." (S079, c.1997)
  - Films now play on phones and 20-meter screens and are cut as if they were the same, which causes dissonance in cutting rate (paraphrase, S025, 2015-11).
  - VR: "It's like cinema was in 1897. And and we can't predict where it's really going to go." (S051, 2016-09) "you as the director cannot control what the audience is going to look at and you can't control the eye lines so to speak which is the bread and butter of cinematography" (S050, 2020-03)

## Financing and distribution of small films (7 sources)
- **Stance:** Small and documentary films earn little and struggle for distribution without a studio. One festival win can open the doors. Risk your own money boldly or not at all.
- **Evidence:**
  - "I think there's very little money in documentary filmmaking" (S051, 2016-09)
  - Particle Fever: "the film was turned down by film festivals. There was no studio behind it." (S076, undated) After the Sheffield audience award: "And after that, doors opened up." (S076)
  - Her Name Was Moviola: "we crowdfunded it for 30,000 lb" (S058, 2025-05) "We've not had any luck with getting distribution for it at this point." (S058, 2025-05)
  - On Coppola's own money: "part of you gets very conservative like I have to get my money back and Francis did just the opposite" (S052, 2016-03)
  - Timing: Jarhead (2005) was about the 1990 Gulf War, but "events overcame this film because it was about a war in the Gulf in 1990" (S075, undated); Particle Fever got its ending when the Higgs announcement came during the edit (S039).

## Metrics and forecasting post (7 sources)
- **Stance:** He runs post on a few numbers of thumb, and says plainly that they are guides, not laws.
- **Evidence:**
  - "an audience can process only two and a half thematic elements at any moment" (S071, 2005-11) "a sustained action scene averages out to fourteen new camera positions a minute" (S071, 2005-11)
  - "within 10 days of shooting I have a very good idea of how long the first assembly" (S050, 2020-03)
  - "In general, at the moment of a transition, the last shot of the outgoing scene is held 30 % longer than it would if it were a cut within the body of the scene." (S081, undated)
  - Rule of Six weights: emotion 51%, story 23%, rhythm 10%, eye trace 7%, 2D plane 5%, 3D space 4% (S067). "The values I put after each item are slightly tongue-in-cheek," (S067, 2025-03)
  - "we have intuitions about some of this but we don't have a engineering handbook for this kind of stuff" (S049, 2020-10)
- **Over time:** his split for a silent cut once sound is turned on: 2016-03, 70% fine, 10% wrong, 15% happy accidents: "But another 15% will actually be really interesting, because it happened by chance." (S012) 2026-10 (newer): 70% right, 15% wrong, 15% fortuitous: "exactly the way it should be. 15% is just wrong." (S057)

## Music: temp tracks, composers and how much (7 sources)
- **Stance:** Music should channel emotion the drama already made, not manufacture it. Avoid temp music if you can; bring the composer in early; keep the freedom to use no music; for real tension, use none.
- **Evidence:**
  - "if you use music to create the emotion, rather than to modulate or channel emotion already created by the drama itself, you are using music the way athletes use steroids" (S002, 2005)
  - "the best solution is not to have temp music at all but we don't live in that world all the time" (S050, 2020-03) "the music and the film start to mix up their DNA" (S055, 2018-06)
  - "if you gave me a magic wand I would say the composure should be on the film during shooting" (S050, 2020-03)
  - "Ideally, the amount and placement of music in a film should be such that the filmmakers have the freedom to use music or not at any particular moment." (S002, 2005)
  - "you want music to be kind of Sideways from what it is that you're looking at" (S052, 2016-03)
  - "well there's no music you're you're on your own baby and that's ultimately much more scary" (S055, 2018-06)
- **In practice:** he does temp, by intuition: "My intuitions are good." (S019, 2020-01)

## Disagreeing with the director (6 sources)
- **Stance:** An editor is paid for ideas. Pitch a real idea, raise it again later, try a third time if it matters, then drop it. The director has the last word.
- **Evidence:**
  - "My rule of thumb for places where there's a disagreement between you, the editor, and the director is another rule of three." (S053, 2025-03)
  - "If it’s REALLY important to you, try it a third time." (S018, 2020-03) "What you’re being paid for is to contribute ideas" (S018, 2020-03)
  - "it's your job, your duty to really stick up for some idea, but don't beat it to death, basically." (S053, 2025-03)
  - "if the director sees it and overrules it, that's the director's prerogative" (S079, c.1997)
  - "My job is to be the person who challenges the director and bring the real vision out of hiding." (S035, 2013-07)
  - When Coppola proposed shelving The Conversation: "i said i have a couple of ideas let's not shell the film let me do these ideas and see what happens" (S049, 2020-10)

## Before the shoot: script, timing and vendors (6 sources)
- **Stance:** Read the script before signing, time it with a stopwatch, send the director notes, and check that vendors can meet the standard. A strong script survives what the shoot and edit do to it.
- **Evidence:**
  - "I also time the screenplay." (S017, 2020-02) It takes about two days and feeds a database that predicts the assembly (S050).
  - "my technique for reading is to read at speed so I don't stop" (S050, 2020-03)
  - Notes as "just top-of-the-head ideas about where I was engaged or where I was a little confused when I read the screenplay" (S017, 2020-02)
  - "A really great screenplay has to be almost indifferent to what happens to it." (S018, 2020-03) "you can think of a screenplay as a hologram that no matter what abuse it receives, it somehow preserves some of the original elements" (S056, 2022-02)
  - "I don't want to rearrange a script everyone liked." (S029, 2009-10)
  - "Is the lab up to developing and printing over a million feet of negative to the standards of John Seale, who is an Academy Award-winning DP?" (S073, 2003-12)

## Sound budget and where to spend it (6 sources)
- **Stance:** Sound is the cheapest way to add scale, so spend creatively there when the picture budget is thin. Spend real money only where the audience can register it.
- **Evidence:**
  - "If you use it creatively, sound can punch way above its weight." (S026, 2017-08)
  - "it's much less expensive than image and it sneaks into the audience's mind sideways." (S020, 2024-03)
  - "the budget for sound will inevitably diminish" (S054, 2019-10), because shooting overruns squeeze post.
  - When the film can afford it: "when somebody fired an AK-47, it should be an AK-47 with real bullets in it" (S006, 2016-02)
  - Against overkill: "going in with a thousand lights for a single set" (S079, c.1997)
  - On syncing every footstep in a crowd: "You have paid too much attention to something that the mind is incapable of assimilating anyway, even if it wanted to." (S002, 2005)

## Work hours and physical method (6 sources)
- **Stance:** Long hours come with the job and suit a certain temperament. Stand, walk and take breaks to stay sharp.
- **Evidence:**
  - "I gravitated toward it immediately because of just something about my personality that it being locked in a room for 14 hours a day" (S053, 2025-03)
  - "Walking to work is important." (S053, 2025-03)
  - "I believe every editor should stand to edit. That’s just my particular soapbox." (S067, 2025-03) "That's why I stand when I edit, to feel this rhythm." (S035, 2013-07)
  - When stuck, switch scenes: "There's always something to do in some other area of the film" (S053, 2025-03)
  - A good editor needs endurance for 16-hour days in a stuffy room (paraphrase, S025, 2015-11).

## The editor's outside eye: off the set, apart from the director (6 sources)
- **Stance:** Stay off the set so you meet the footage as the audience will. A separate editor sees what an immersed director cannot.
- **Evidence:**
  - "I want to protect my innocence so that I can transmit that to the audience unencumbered by my knowledge of how angry everyone was with each other that day." (S011, 2005-11)
  - "So by keeping five or six steps away from that process I think I'm working to the best of my abilities." (S011, 2005-11)
  - "One of the obligations of the editor is to be the ombudsman, so to speak, of the audience." (S020, 2024-03)
  - "There is only one first time, and it is important to preserve that feeling, which is as close as you will ever get to the feeling the audience will have when they see it." (S017, 2020-02)
  - "The editor has the ability to lend a guiding hand in the direction of the story that a director, who is so immersed in the shots, may not see." (S029, 2009-10) He grants that some directors, such as the Coens, edit their own films well (S029).
  - On Apocalypse Now he was present for two of about 230 shooting days: "I did breathe the air of the Philippine location and catch the mood" (S006, 2016-02)

## Cutting scenes the director loves (5 sources)
- **Stance:** Some scenes are the umbilical cord that got the maker into the film; once their nutrients are in, they can go. Test by removing the scene that seems most essential. Write down why something fails, because you may need it back.
- **Evidence:**
  - "certain scenes are heart scenes and other scenes are like umbilical cords." (S017, 2020-02)
  - "you should be suspicious of those very scenes and wonder if this film can ride the bike without these training wheels." (S025, 2015-11)
  - "So there’s the editorial equivalent of that, where we cut out the very scene that seemed to be most important just to learn what the other scenes around it are contributing." (S017, 2020-02)
  - "the film closed over it it's it's as if it never existed" (S050, 2020-03) "it could be snipped out without creating problems later on" (S058, 2025-05)
  - "So if you think something is not working, write down why it’s not working, because that might be the very thing that you have to get back to." (S017, 2020-02)

## Fixing script and shoot problems in post (5 sources)
- **Stance:** Post can rescue a film, often with one shot, one line or a sound, but deferring decisions has a price, and the mix is the last chance.
- **Evidence:**
  - "having too many deferred decisions is like not paying your taxes for ten years" (S079, c.1997)
  - "re-recording mixers have to be sensitive to the fact that this is the last time the director can solve any of the problems in the film" (S049, 2020-10)
  - "I can't solve this problem visually, but maybe I can solve it with sound." (S020, 2024-03)
  - The Conversation with a fifth of its scenes unshot: "In the end, it came down to one shot." (S053, 2025-03)
  - "you try to minimize what seem like mistakes and maximize the potential of everything else." (S018, 2020-03)

## Documentary truth and manipulation (5 sources)
- **Stance:** All editing manipulates; a documentary may bend, but not much, and every claim needs sources and a visual. Pick whose story it is rather than pretending to a god's-eye view.
- **Evidence:**
  - "The very fact that you do editing at all and the very fact that you choose to point the camera in this direction and not that direction is a manipulation." (S033, 2013-06)
  - "In documentary, you’re clearly obligated to not bend things too much." (S034, undated) "to not bend things at all would make a film like this impossible because the physical representation of this world is so small." (S034)
  - "at every opportunity, made sure that we had multiple sources for everything that is said and had visuals to back it up." (S013, 2020-08)
  - "we couldn’t pretend to take a God’s-eye-view of what the truth of this was." (S019, 2020-01)
  - Folding two real events into one scene in Particle Fever: "And so could we fold these two things together and make it seem as if he was there?" (S051, 2016-09)

## Burnout and the end of a project (5 sources)
- **Stance:** The end of a long edit brings a seasickness that is internal and passes. Rest the mind with an unrelated craft, and stop hammering at problems.
- **Evidence:**
  - "It’s the equivalent, I think, to a kind of sea sickness." (S025, 2015-11) "you can kind of endure it again just like seasickness" (S050, 2020-03)
  - "you work with great intensity, and then it suddenly stops. And you don't know that you'll ever work again" (S051, 2016-09)
  - Translating Malaparte between films: "it was a way of sort of taking methadone after heroin" (S051, 2016-09)
  - "If you hammer away too consciously at a problem, you’re in danger of over-articulating the decisions." (S016, 2020-04)
  - Switching from picture to sound: "there's a awkward period of about a week or two weeks where you think well there's nothing to do" (S055, 2018-06)

## Explaining versus trusting the audience (5 sources)
- **Stance:** Leave one question open. A film that explains everything has no room for the audience, who finish it.
- **Evidence:**
  - "A film that answers all of its questions, that resolves itself completely on its own terms, really doesn't need an audience." (S051, 2016-09)
  - "And really the last creative act of any film is viewing by the audience." (S025, 2015-11)
  - "you have to find ways to reintroduce ambiguity. Otherwise, the film will just crush the ambiguity out of the subject matter." (S056, 2022-02)
  - On over-explaining: "And that's effective, as far as it goes, but I don't think you're getting under the skin of the audience when you do that." (S020, 2024-03)
  - "the responsibility of filmmakers is to find ways within that completeness to refrain from achieving it." (S004, undated)

## Branching out: directing and two hats (5 sources)
- **Stance:** He tried directing once and it ended his directing path; he is content as editor and sound designer. Watching others direct is not doing it.
- **Over time:**
  - After Return to Oz (1985) he kept trying to direct for three to five years, then: "I had a family to support and kids going to school, and I couldn't sustain it." (S026, 2017-08)
  - 2012-08: "No, I’m happy doing what I do." (S066)
  - 2025-05 (newer): "none of that learned experience filtered through to the visceral experience of actually directing a multi-million dollar film" (S058) and "It's a little late to be directing your very first film." (S058)
- **Also:** on doing sound and picture on the same film: "I don't think I did wear two hats simultaneously" (S055, 2018-06). Disney's neglect of Return to Oz gave him more control, not less (paraphrase, S025).

## Previews and test screenings (4 sources)
- **Stance:** Previews show your blind spots. When the audience complains about one place, the cause often sits somewhere else.
- **Evidence:**
  - "What a preview does is emotionally move you 90 degrees off-center." (S017, 2020-02)
  - "the problem is not in the elbow. It’s somewhere else." (S017, 2020-02)
  - "it was clear from the previews that the audience had had a hard time getting traction at the beginning of the film" (S058, 2025-05)
  - Cold Mountain: "It was not working as it was written and audiences were emotionally confused." (S081, undated) He added snow shots from other material to give them time.
  - A great preview can scare a studio (S059, see Studios above).

## AI in the cutting room (4 sources)
- **Stance:** Big and unknown. His working line: assemble the film yourself so you know it, then ask the machine for alternatives and keep what is good.
- **Over time:**
  - 2020-03: "yeah it's already happening" (S050), about a program that recut home movies in set styles.
  - 2025-03: "Uh I don't, as Chairman Mao said, it's too early to tell." (S053) "hold on to your hats, guys, because it's going to be another big, it's like the coming of sound in the sense." (S053) "I haven't used it other than the text AI." (S053)
  - 2025-05: "when you assemble a film yourself you learn the film." (S058) "It may be that you do the assembly and then you put it in and you say do this a different way." (S058) Risk: "AI fingerprints on it that kind of give it a certain kind of smell that is not your smell" (S058). "Now you have to in a sense reinvent the method for every new film you work on. And AI is going to complicate that in spades." (S058)
  - 2026-10 (newer): "We just don't know." (S057) "AI is television cubed because it's affecting how we fight war." (S057)
- **Limit:** he flags his own view as early: "I'm inventing stuff here because it's early early days" (S058, 2025-05).

## Will new tools save time on post? (4 sources)
- **Stance:** No. Tools let you do more in the same time and defer decisions; work grows to fill the space.
- **Over time:**
  - c.1997: "saving time is fine in theory, but in practice it usually doesn't work that way." (S079)
  - 2006-06: the economics against turning the camera off are gone, so editors face more hours of footage (paraphrase, S024).
  - 2025-03: "work expands to fill the area available" (S053), said of why cheaper tools have not made post cheaper.
  - 2026-10 (newer, and softer): in the digital era you can work as fast as you can think (paraphrase, S057).
- **Read:** faster tools raise ambition and footage, not margins. Inferred from S024, S053, S079.

## ADR and replacing production sound (4 sources)
- **Stance:** Replace bad production sound without fear, schedule it by arithmetic, and dirty clean ADR so it plays as real.
- **Evidence:**
  - "in general I schedule about eight lines of ADR per hour of recording time" (S050, 2020-03)
  - Apocalypse Now: "I'll say 92% of the film is ADR uh the sound from the set was unusable" (S052, 2016-03); elsewhere "I’m guessing 98 percent of it is ADR." (S006, 2016-02). The figures differ.
  - "I made good ADR sound not so good in order to make it sound more like production dialogue" (S052, 2016-03)
  - "so do anything you can to get rid of the microphone presence" (S050, 2020-03)

## Pacing, cutting rate and long takes (4 sources)
- **Stance:** Do not feed the audience faster than it can digest. Fast cutting in bursts is fine; as a house style it costs comprehension. Long unbroken takes have a short shelf life.
- **Evidence:**
  - "if you feed people too fast, they feel like the stuff is being rammed down their throat and they’re going to choke." (S018, 2020-03)
  - "you can do that, but you lose comprehensibility" (S025, 2015-11)
  - "And humor, such as it is, is a very good digestive agent." (S018, 2020-03)
  - "it has a limited shelf life in my feeling" (S049, 2020-10), on long-take films such as 1917.

## Credit and the editor as writer (3 sources)
- **Stance:** In documentary the editor co-writes the film and deserves writing credit.
- **Evidence:**
  - Asked whether documentary editors deserve writing credit: "Yes, I absolutely feel that, having done it." (S019, 2020-01)
  - "The editor of a documentary is helping to write the story" (S016, 2020-04)
  - "Whereas on a documentary, you are deciding what notes are going to get played in the first place." (S019, 2020-01)
  - He repeats it in 2026 (paraphrase, S057).

## Competition and entering the market (3 sources)
- **Stance:** Tools are now nearly free, so everyone can cut and the field is crowded; the edge is dedication. Start by making something.
- **Evidence:**
  - "The bad news is everybody can do that. Everybody in the world can do that." (S058, 2025-05)
  - "The good news is that the tools that you have are completely accessible to you now for almost nothing." (S058, 2025-05)
  - "back 60 years ago, we didn't have competition" (S058, 2025-05) "So, we we entered filmmaking at a stable era." (S058)
  - "Film editing is now something almost everyone can do at a simple level and enjoy it, but to take it to a higher level requires the same dedication and persistence that any art form does." (S067, 2025-03)
  - For newcomers: "short-term pessimistic, long-term optimistic" (S057, 2026-10)

## Getting fired and taking over someone else's film (3 sources)
- **Stance:** A firing is often a message to someone else, and a replaced editor is rarely the real problem. Take over only to help a friend, and not for long.
- **Evidence:**
  - Tomorrowland: "The studio had the gun, I was the chicken, and Brad was the monkey." (S016, 2020-04) "sometimes you have to kill the chicken to scare the monkey and in this case I was the chicken and Brad was the monkey" (S050, 2020-03)
  - "it usually has absolutely nothing to do with the talents of big previous editor" (S050, 2020-03); the cause is usually friction between producer, studio and director (S050).
  - "it's usually to help a friend" (S050, 2020-03) "you are the grim reaper who comes in when to take over the corpse of a dying film you know" (S050)

## Choosing which projects to take (2 sources)
- **Stance:** Three legs: the material resonates and pushes you, the director and team fit, and there is enough time and money. Any two are almost enough; a missing leg is a warning. No script, no deal.
- **Evidence:**
  - "those three things are important any two of those are almost enough" (S050, 2020-03)
  - On Tomorrowland: "if you can't give me the script there must be problems with it but I didn't say that" (S050, 2020-03) "I made a judgement and it turned out to be the wrong judgement" (S050)
  - His usual start: "We had lunch and we exchanged ideas, and I got the screenplay." (S075, undated)

## Pricing, fees and discounting
- **No recorded position.** He never discusses his rates or discounts. Nearest: an executive's anger can be theater meant to make you lower your ask (S057, 2026-10, see Studios above).

## Debt
- **No recorded position.** Nearest: Coppola risking his own money and not turning cautious (S052, 2016-03).

## Equity, partners and selling the company
- **No recorded position.** Nearest: he, Coppola and Lucas left Hollywood for San Francisco to escape its business-level divisions (S077, 2019-04), and he made a pact with Lucas over a Warner Bros. scholarship (paraphrase, S079).

## Paid ads, marketing and personal brand
- **No recorded position.** Nearest: he dislikes editing rooms covered in posters of past films: "it’s bragging, or so it seems to me." (S017, 2020-02); and "Editors are notoriously closed-mouth about what they do because they’re kind of like the priest in the confessional" (S016, 2020-04).

## Episodic television and series editing
- **No recorded position.** Every case in the corpus is a feature or feature documentary. His length rules (30% assembly overrun, two-hour limit) come from features; applying them to episodes is a guess, not his view.
